frozen_candidate_root_contribution: The root marks water (a potable-substance) as carrying an intense, biting bitter-salt harshness — the quality of being so pungently briny that it repels consumption. It is the negative sensory pole of drinkable water: the property of being harsh/undrinkable rather than merely "salt as a substance."

internal_discovery.candidate_root_contribution: The root marks water (a potable-substance) as carrying an intense, biting bitter-salt harshness — the quality of being so pungently briny that it repels consumption. It is the negative sensory pole of drinkable water: the property of being harsh/undrinkable rather than merely "salt as a substance."
internal_discovery.plain_explanation: Every one of the three occurrences is the same lexeme أُجَاج (ujāj), all tagged form N, and all predicated of water. In 25:53:10:1 and 35:12:11:1 the word stands in an explicit antithetical pair: one sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ (sweet, fresh) — in 35:12 further glossed سَآئِغٌ شَرَابُهُ (its drink slips down pleasantly) — and the other is مِلْحٌ أُجَاجٌ. Crucially أُجَاج is appended AFTER مِلْح (salt): the substance-word "salt" is already present, so أُجَاج is not supplying the bare fact of salt but intensifying/qualifying it as bitingly briny and undrinkable. In 56:70:4:1 the word appears alone, without مِلْح: "if We willed We could have made it (the water they drink, from the preceding verse) أُجَاجًا, so why are you not grateful?" Here أُجَاج by itself carries the whole load — spoiled, undrinkable brine set against the freshwater they actually receive. Across all three, subtracting the drinkable/fresh counterpart leaves one invariant: the root contributes the harsh bitter-salt quality that makes water unfit to drink.
internal_discovery.layer_separation_note: FORM: all three are the same nominal/adjectival form (QAC N), the pattern فُعَال describing an inherent quality; no verbs, participles, or contrasting derivatives exist to cross-check, so morphology adds only "quality/property nominal" — subtracting it leaves the quality itself. CONSTRUCTION: two tokens are attributive (مِلْحٌ أُجَاجٌ, adjective on the head noun "salt"); one is a predicative object of جَعَلَ (جَعَلْنَٰهُ أُجَاجًا, "made it ujāj") — subtracting the attribution-vs-predication frame leaves the same quality. PARTICIPANTS: the described entity is always water/sea (البحرين / البحران / the implied drinking-water of 56:68) — subtract to leave a substance-independent (within data, water-bound) sensory property. CONTEXT: all sit in sign-of-creation / gratitude discourse (تَأْكُلُونَ… تَشْكُرُونَ; فَلَوْلَا تَشْكُرُونَ) — this rhetorical framing is subtracted as context, not root meaning. Residue after all subtractions: biting bitter-salt undrinkable harshness of water.
internal_discovery.strongest_counterexample: 56:70:4:1 (جَعَلْنَٰهُ أُجَاجًا) is the hardest because it lacks the مِلْح ("salt") that anchors the sense in the other two, and because it is a predicate of جَعَلَ rather than an attribute — one could worry the meaning is being imported from the sister verses. It reconciles cleanly: the immediately preceding verses (56:68-69) speak of the fresh water they drink and its heaven-sent source, so أُجَاج stands as the antithetical spoiled/undrinkable outcome. That the word alone, without مِلْح, still denotes undrinkable brine actually strengthens the residue — it shows the harsh-briny-unfitness is carried by the root itself and not borrowed from the noun "salt."
internal_discovery.competing_hypothesis: The strongest alternative is that the root simply means "salty" (the substance/quality of salt), with the fresh/salt contrast doing all the work. Internal evidence arbitrates against pure equivalence: in 25:53 and 35:12 the substance-word مِلْح ("salt") is already stated, and أُجَاج is added on top of it. If the root meant only "salt," the pairing مِلْح أُجَاج would be redundant; its presence signals an intensifying/qualifying layer — bitter, burning, undrinkable brininess beyond plain salinity. 56:70's solitary أُجَاج confirms the root can carry "undrinkable brine" without leaning on مِلْح. So the data favor "harsh bitter-salt unfitness" over bare "salty," though with only three tokens the exact conceptual weighting (saltiness-intensity vs. bitterness/burning) remains somewhat underdetermined.
internal_discovery.distinctiveness_note: Nearest semantic neighbors: مِلْح (m-l-H, the substance salt/salinity as such), عَذْب (E-*-b, sweet/palatable), فُرَات (f-r-t, sweet fresh drinkable water), and a general "bitter" root like مرّ (m-r-r). Ajj is distinct from مِلْح: مِلْح names the salt substance, whereas أُجَاج names the sensory harshness/undrinkable intensity layered onto it (hence مِلْح أُجَاج is non-redundant). It is the polar opposite of عَذْب/فُرَات/سَآئِغ (the drinkable-sweet cluster). Falsifiability: if a confirmed occurrence applied a derivative of Ajj to something sweet, pleasant, or freely drinkable — or used it purely to denote the salt substance with no harsh/repellent/undrinkable force — the proposed residue would be falsified.
internal_discovery.rationale: A single non-empty contribution — the biting bitter-salt undrinkable harshness of water — is surface-recoverable in all three occurrences without forcing, and it stands in a determinate, consistent direction (the negative pole against عَذْب/فُرَات/سَآئِغ). It is sharply distinguishable from the neighbor root مِلْح, since أُجَاج is stacked onto مِلْح in two of three cases and carries undrinkable-brine sense alone in the third, showing the residue belongs to the root rather than to "salt." These features argue toward STRONG. I hold the rating at MODERATE rather than STRONG for two honest reasons: (1) the entire evidence base is one lexeme (أُجَاج) in one morphological form with no derivational variation, so the root's contribution cannot be triangulated across form-families — root and lexeme cannot be fully separated; and (2) the precise conceptual center is mildly underdetermined between "intense saltiness" and "bitter/burning harshness," a distinction three water-bound tokens cannot settle. No occurrence is contradicted or absent, so none appears in inconsistent_refs, and the disposition is PREFERRED.

adversarial_verification.notes: Refutation attempt failed to break the unity. All 3 confirmed occurrences are the identical lexeme أُجَاج (form N), all predicated of water, all denoting the harsh, biting, bitter-salt quality that makes water undrinkable. 25:53:10:1 and 35:12:11:1 place it in explicit antithesis to عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ (fresh/sweet), and 35:12 glosses the fresh counterpart as سَآئِغٌ شَرَابُهُ (drink slips down pleasantly) — the drinkability axis is textually explicit. 56:70:4:1 has أُجَاجًا standing alone (no مِلْح) yet carries the same "spoiled/undrinkable brine" load against the freshwater actually given. Hardest case = 56:70, where absence of مِلْح raises the worry that أُجَاج might mean only generic "undrinkable/bitter" rather than "salt-harsh"; resolved by (a) classical lexical value of أُجَاج as intensely salty-bitter undrinkable water and (b) the two paired verses independently licensing the salt-harshness reading. DISTINCTIVENESS: cleanly discriminates against the nearest neighbor مِلْح (salt-as-substance) — decisively because in 25:53 and 35:12 مِلْح already supplies "salt" and أُجَاج is appended AFTER it, so it cannot be redundant substance-marking; it must be the intensifying harsh/undrinkable-quality pole. FALSIFIABILITY: clear failure condition (any occurrence of fresh/drinkable water, non-water, or bare salt-substance under this root); none met. CAVEAT (not disqualifying, not a failing occurrence): data is only 3 tokens of one lexeme in one form, so cross-form robustness is untestable and unity is partly a data artifact — but nothing within scope contradicts the candidate. No genuine failing occurrences found; verdict SUPPORTED.
